title: A day of factors
hookLine: noticing mental factors through a whole ordinary day

lines: THE ALARM, THE KETTLE, THE HEADLINE.
cards: The alarm goes off. A flash of something: dread, or relief that it's Saturday. The kettle.
A headline on the phone, and the jaw tightens. A message from a friend, and it loosens. The car won't start, or the toddler won't wear the blue socks.
A long meeting where the mind wanders out the window. A kind word from a stranger at the store. Dishes.
Bed. Nobody would call that day a meditation. But every one of those moments had factors in it, the same ones the Abhidhamma lists.

teach.b: First, the suttas already point here. In the great teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, attention doesn't stop when the sitting stops.

In paraphrase: going out and coming back, looking ahead and looking around, bending and stretching, putting on the robe, eating, drinking, chewing, even in the bathroom, the practitioner acts with clear knowing.
Getting dressed counts. Lunch counts. Second, the Abhidhamma gives that clear knowing something to look for.
Remember the seven factors it says are in every moment of mind: contact, feeling, perception, intention, one-pointedness, life, attention. So there's never a moment with nothing to notice.
The kettle has contact and feeling in it. So does the headline. Third, the colors change through the day.
Some moments carry restlessness or envy or dullness. Others carry calm, gladness, a flicker of compassion.

teach.h: THE MIND IS MORE LIKE WEATHER.
teach.b: Watched across a whole day, the mind looks less like one fixed mood and more like weather: a squall at nine, sun at noon, fog in the afternoon meeting.
That's what the lists have been saying all along: mind is many, and each state passes. Fourth, a simple tool.
Once an hour, stop for one breath and ask: what three factors are here right now? Maybe tired, curious, a little irritated. Maybe hungry, focused, glad.
You don't need the Pali names, and you don't need to get it right. By evening you'd have a small map of one day, drawn from the inside.

how: Some meditation teachers ask students to bring mindfulness into daily tasks such as walking, eating and washing, and some monasteries ring a bell during the day as a reminder to return to the present moment.

games.q: what does “a day of factors” mean?
o: a whole day set aside for a sitting retreat
a calendar of the year's Buddhist holy days
noticing the mind's factors all through the day

games.q: a day of noticing: tap the pairs.
p: eating, dressing, walking with clear knowing
present in every moment of mind

s: in the suttas, mindfulness is only for formal sitting
the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness includes eating, drinking, getting dressed and walking.
the Abhidhamma lists some factors present in every moment of mind
contact, feeling, perception, intention, one-pointedness, life and attention.
you need the Pali names to notice factors through the day
tired, curious, irritated: plain words work. you don't need to get it right.

games.q: your hourly reminder goes off in the middle of a tense phone call. what does a day of noticing ask?
o: one breath, and name what's here
ignore it until the day is calmer
games.why: the suttas include every activity, not only the calm ones. one breath, three factors, and back to the call.

practice: Take a few easy breaths and ask: what three factors are here right now?
Wait for them instead of hunting: maybe a feeling, pleasant or unpleasant or neither, maybe a mood like boredom or ease, maybe attention itself, landing on the breath.
Name all three quietly, then let them go and sit with the breath.

wordCard.voice: A day of factors. Carrying the Abhidhamma's mirror through an ordinary day, and noticing which factors come and go, from the alarm to bedtime. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a day of noticing. From the alarm to the dishes, no moment is empty of something to see. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 22 (Mahasatipatthana Sutta), clear comprehension in all activities
Abhidhammattha Sangaha II (the universal mental factors)
